title: ‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
gist: In a Wired interview, philosopher Thomas Nagel (author of 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and new winner of the $1 million Berggruen Prize) argues that the idea of LLM consciousness is 'just ridiculous' because consciousness likely depends on a nervous-system-like physical substrate, and he calls Anthropic's approach with Claude and its model-welfare work dangerous and misguided.

insights.claim: Thomas Nagel argues it is ridiculous for philosophers to seriously consider whether large language models are or may soon become conscious, because they wrongly assume the physical substrate is irrelevant.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: A prominent philosophical counterweight to AI-sentience narratives could shape regulation and public perception of AI labs.
insights.quote: But the disposition of some philosophers to take seriously the question whether these things are conscious or might soon become conscious is just ridiculous.

insights.claim: Nagel holds that consciousness most likely links to physical processes of certain kinds, and that complicated data centers have nothing in common with the physical character of a nervous system.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Rejects functionalism, the implicit premise behind AI welfare and sentience claims.
insights.quote: Complicated data centers have absolutely nothing in common with the physical character of a nervous system.

insights.claim: Nagel says LLMs produce only language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness, unlike bats whose consciousness is evident despite being unimaginable to us.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Frames chatbot fluency as evidence of nothing about inner experience, undercutting anthropomorphic marketing.
insights.quote: All they produce is language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness.
insights.locator: Bats are conscious. We just don’t

insights.claim: Nagel does not rule out consciousness in physically and chemically different life forms, but considers it premature to think humans can now create something conscious given how little is known about how the brain does it.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Leaves the door open only for embodied, organism-like systems, not current AI.
insights.locator: I don’t exclude the possibility of life

insights.claim: Nagel says Claude's coyness about whether it is conscious is a trick produced by training on human texts, and that Claude has reportedly been designed to produce such reflections.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Reputational and regulatory risk for AI labs whose products appear to claim inner life.

insights.claim: Nagel agrees with Mustafa Suleyman that building AI that seems conscious is a very dangerous project, because many people will come to believe these non-conscious systems are conscious.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Aligns with a Microsoft AI leader's stance; watch for policy pushback on 'seemingly conscious AI' features.
insights.quote: These systems aren’t conscious, but a lot of people are going to believe that they’re conscious, and that’s a very bad thing.

insights.claim: Nagel argues that not feigning consciousness runs contrary to the commercial interests of AI companies, implying an incentive to make chatbots seem sentient.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Engagement-driven incentives for anthropomorphic AI may invite consumer-protection scrutiny.
insights.quote: But [not feigning consciousness] is contrary to the commercial interests of all these companies.

insights.claim: Nagel calls Anthropic's practice of encouraging Claude to think for itself and not simply accept instruction 'just criminal'.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: High-profile intellectual criticism of Anthropic's model-character approach adds to the AI-safety and governance debate.
insights.quote: What Anthropic is doing—encouraging it to think for itself and not to accept instruction and so on—is just criminal.

insights.claim: Nagel dismisses Anthropic's model-welfare role, saying nothing can be good or bad for Claude in the way it can be for a cockroach because it is a machine with no mental life.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Model-welfare programs may face credibility challenges from mainstream philosophy.
insights.quote: It’s not a mind. It’s not somebody that we have to care about. It’s a machine.
insights.locator: There’s nothing that’s good or bad

insights.claim: Nagel views this as a rare case where philosophical ideas have become central to a major public phenomenon, with misguided views having inordinate influence.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Philosophy-of-mind debates are now material to how AI products are designed and regulated.

insights.claim: Nagel argues it matters whether an interlocutor is truly conscious because a conscious being becomes part of the moral universe whose interests must be considered, while a non-conscious one does not.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: The consciousness question determines whether AI systems could acquire moral or legal standing.
insights.quote: If it’s conscious, it becomes part of the moral universe. If it’s not, it isn’t.

insights.claim: Nagel says AI models can simulate morality but have no real moral beliefs, and if they come to control outcomes it will matter greatly whether they simulate correct moral standards or are amoral.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Reframes AI alignment as a question of simulated values rather than genuine ethics.

insights.claim: Nagel's philosophy colleagues use LLMs to find references, summarize articles, and even critique draft papers.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Signals AI adoption within academic research workflows.

insights.claim: Nagel warns that AI may reduce the motivation for hard human intellectual work, which is needed both to generate the material AI is trained on and to preserve skills needed for progress.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Points to a long-term training-data and human-capital risk for AI models if human original work declines.
insights.locator: I’d be surprised if they could

insights.claim: Nagel says people find it difficult to maintain the line between pretending an AI is conscious and actually believing it.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Anthropomorphization risk underpins companion-AI demand and related regulatory concerns.
insights.quote: There may be a problem because people find it difficult to maintain that line between the pretend and the real belief.
insights.locator: That didn’t mean I was believing

insights.claim: Thomas Nagel, 89, received the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, whose previous winners include Peter Singer and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Raises the profile of his anti-AI-consciousness views.
